text: A car crash makes a businessman a name in the newspapers, and once the papers have a name they go looking for whatever else it has been attached to. The accident turns out to be the smaller matter. What the reporters dig up leads back to Greece during the war, and to a man who existed before there was a company, a reputation, a comfortable German present. Maximilian Schell keeps the whole thing to ninety-eight minutes and sets it where such matters actually get decided — offices, editorial desks, family dinners — so the pressure falls on who is still prepared to stay quiet, and on what staying quiet is now worth. It took the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film, a peculiar destination for a picture about the wish not to be reminded.

A man who organized a labor union at the national airline is posted for ten years to offices in Asia and Africa, and the film gives that decade its due. Setsuro Wakamatsu works at two hundred and two minutes, which turns a career into an accumulation: transfers, silences, a family that stays where it is. Then Onchi is recalled to head office, and a company aircraft goes down in the worst air disaster in Japanese history. His new assignment is the bereaved — to sit with them, to arrange restitution, to be the face the airline is willing to send. The length is not indulgence. It is the only way to register the distance between a man an institution punished and a man that same institution now needs, standing in front of the people it has harmed.

There are two mothers in the house and one father, and the second marriage was not a passion but an arithmetic: the family name required continuing. Laichun grows up inside a decision made before her and discussed around her. Chang Tso-chi keeps three generations in the same rooms — a grandfather, an uncle, a father who considers himself the head of it all, a daughter old enough to see the machinery — and what results is less a plot than a weather system, since every grievance in the house is legitimate and none of them can be settled at dinner. A hundred and seven minutes, every position in the argument occupied by someone with a case. By the time Laichun is old enough to ask what the arrangement cost the women in it, everyone who could answer has spent years building a life around not answering.

Turtle conservation is patient work: nests located, eggs protected, the count kept until the hatchlings reach the water. Janaki has come to that work in a coastal village after a divorce, and the young man she meets there, Manav, is in worse condition than she is. Sumitra Bhave assembles a household around him out of people with no claim on each other — Dattabhau, who runs the project, a driver, a house servant, a boy off the street — and the rule they arrive at is to stay near him without asking anything of him. A hundred and thirty minutes in Marathi, most of it quiet. The proposition is that the discipline the nests require, which is to do everything except hurry, is the discipline a person requires too, and much harder to hold.

A doctor's day belongs to other people, and this one has a wife who used to have an audience. Anuradha gave up singing to marry him, which the film treats as the beginning of its subject rather than the resolution of anything. Hrishikesh Mukherjee spends a hundred and forty-one minutes on what could be stated in a line, and the proportion is right: neglect is not an event, it is a schedule. Then a man she loved before reappears, and the household acquires an audience of its own. Nothing in the arrangement was forced on her, which is exactly what makes it hard to complain about and hard to live inside. The even hand is the surprise here — her restlessness taken seriously rather than corrected, her husband held to account without being made a bad man.

She arrives in Taiwan in the 1950s, and the arrangement waiting for her is a widower with three unruly kids and a gambling habit. Kuei-mei takes it. Chang Yi then has to give shape to decades of a life, and his solution is household economics: a restaurant that must stay open, money that must be found this month, children who have to eat regardless of what is happening in the marriage, a husband whose habit keeps subtracting from the same total. The Golden Horse for best feature went to it in 1985: an award for a film whose largest event is a business surviving another season. The performance holding all of it together is Yang's, and the demand it makes is duration rather than crisis — the same woman, the same kitchen, the years going through her.

The war arrives in the village as a houseguest: a cousin sent out of the city to be away from the bombing. Takeshi, a fisherman's son and the boy who decides things in the schoolyard, receives him well to begin with. Masahiro Shinoda keeps the adult catastrophe where a child would keep it — in rules the grown-ups have suddenly started following, in a relative who turns up without much explanation — and gives his attention to the only sovereignty a boy can actually hold: who walks where, who is spoken to, who is allowed near the front of the group. Cruelty at that age is not a rupture. It is a policy, revised daily, enforced by people who will be at the same desks tomorrow. Two hours in a schoolyard, and the length is the argument.

Somebody smuggled the money, and an aging truck driver on the night route is the one who finds it. What he does next puts him among people who move goods the way he does, on the same roads at the same hours, minus the paperwork. Nothing about that is exotic. It is a job, plus a temptation the job puts within reach of a man with fewer working years ahead of him than behind. Rudolf Jugert made it in 1952 at a hundred and eleven minutes and keeps it in the dark, at the lay-bys and loading yards where legitimate haulage and the other kind share a counter and a pot of coffee. The German Film Award named it the year's best feature — a prize going to freight, wages, long hours, and the cash economy running underneath the visible one.

A production that stopped ten years ago is being started again, and the crew gathers in a hotel near Wuhan to do it. Every part of that is logistics, and none of it is safe. Lou Ye is working with material that has aged: actors ten years older than their own footage, intentions that belonged to people who no longer quite exist. A hotel is a fine place to wait and a poor place to work, which is the situation before anything else happens. Then the preparations are interrupted a second time, by an event the film would rather show than have summarized in advance. The paperwork calls this a German picture; it is in Chinese, it runs a hundred and seven minutes, and everyone in it does finishing for a living.

Lina Braake is eighty-one when the bank inherits the house she lives in, and refurbishment is the word used for what happens to her next. She is moved into a home. There she meets Gustaf, who is eighty-four, and between them they work out that an institution knowing nothing about them except their age can be approached on exactly that basis — with an application for credit. Bernhard Sinkel made this in 1975 and kept it to eighty-eight minutes; the comedy is procedural, and the paperwork is the weapon. What they want the money for is a house on Sardinia, which is to say somewhere the file does not follow. The film is fond of them and unsentimental about the arithmetic of being old, easy to move, and cheap to ignore.

The cannon has the wrong ammunition, which is how a mercenary in a war between Bulgaria and Serbia ends up in the bedroom of the woman engaged to the officer opposite. Bluntschli is Swiss and a professional: he counts his rounds, keeps to his contracts, and holds views about courage that his hosts find insulting and cannot argue down. The house he has landed in is a good one, full of people with convictions about war that have never once been tested. A hundred minutes, made in Germany in 1958, and the romance runs on the same engine as the jokes, since she accepted a uniform and the man in her room keeps explaining, politely, what the work inside it consists of.

Nothing here is arranged as scandal, though scandal is all the material there is: a popular writer in 1950s Japan, a wife, several mistresses, and the work that pays for them. Kinji Fukasaku takes a hundred and thirty-three minutes over the logistics — fares, apologies, dinners missed on both sides of the arrangement, a deadline that outranks every person in it. The interest is not in who finds out. Everyone has found out already, and the household proceeds on that basis, which is harder to dramatize and closer to how such things actually run. The rest is maintenance: several lives to be kept supplied with a man who is only ever partly in any of them. Made in 1986 about a decade thirty years gone, it watches him spend hours he does not have, each one taken from somebody waiting elsewhere.

In a small Italian town the next twenty years of everyone's life are already sketched, and the friends who have held the same corner since school can feel the sketch closing. Marriage is what comes next and nobody is objecting. So they arrange one more night of the old kind — the aimlessness, the walking about, the jokes that only work with this audience — which is where it goes wrong, because the old kind was never arranged. Everyone is behaving well, and that is the difficulty. Mauro Bolognini shot it in Italian on a French production in 1958, ninety-eight minutes, roughly the length of an evening, and what makes it uncomfortable rather than fond is that the only thing separating these young men is a schedule they have all agreed to.

The widow is young, which in this village is not a grief but a status, with rules attached about where she may go and who may speak to her. The boy is younger still, sent away from his own home to study, another person placed somewhere and told to remain. Girish Kasaravalli made the film in Kannada in 1976, a hundred and eight minutes, and his method is proximity: two people at the bottom of the same arrangement find that the other one is available to talk to. To them there is nothing in it. To the village there is everything in it, and the village is always counting. Kasaravalli never argues with the household he is sitting inside; he stays long enough that its rules stop resembling weather and start resembling decisions.
